chapters.title: Identify the carbon bearing halogen
chapters.formula: Aryl C–X and benzylic C–X are different centres
chapters.script: Welcome to Organic Halogens. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. Classify the carbon bearing halogen before comparing reactions. In a haloalkane, halogen is bonded to a saturated carbon. In chlorobenzene, chlorine is directly attached to an aromatic ring carbon. In benzyl chloride, chlorine is attached to a carbon outside the ring, so the reacting environment is different. Primary, secondary and tertiary alkyl halides are classified by how many carbons are attached to the carbon carrying halogen. A carbon halogen bond is generally polarized toward halogen, leaving the carbon susceptible to suitable nucleophiles. Bond strength, leaving group stability, steric access and solvent all affect reactivity. For comparable simple substrates in many substitution settings, iodide is a better leaving group than bromide, which is better than chloride; fluoride is generally poor. This ranking cannot replace a stated mechanism or conditions. Also distinguish allylic and benzylic centres from vinylic and aryl centres. A nearby pi system can stabilize an intermediate, but direct attachment to an unsaturated carbon creates a different substitution problem.
points: CH₃CH₂Cl · Saturated; one C neighbour · Primary haloalkane
C₆H₅CH₂Cl · Outside aromatic ring · Benzylic chloride
C₆H₅Cl · Directly in aromatic ring · Aryl chloride

chapters.title: Preparation and reaction site
chapters.formula: Circle the bond changed by each reagent
chapters.script: Several routes produce organic halides, and they do not all use the same mechanism. Suitable hydrogen halides or reagents such as thionyl chloride can replace an alcohol's hydroxyl group under appropriate conditions. Adding hydrogen halide to an alkene instead consumes a pi bond and adds hydrogen and halogen. Radical halogenation of an alkane uses initiating conditions and can give mixtures. Aromatic ring halogenation commonly uses an electrophilic pathway with a suitable Lewis acid. In toluene, chlorine with iron three chloride under ring substitution conditions can introduce chlorine on the ring, with ortho and para preferences. Under radical conditions such as light, substitution can instead occur at the side chain. Do not infer the reaction site from the molecular formula of the reagent alone. Preparation may also cause elimination, rearrangement or further substitution depending on substrate and conditions. Before writing an arrow, circle the carbon being changed and identify whether the intended process replaces a group, adds across a multiple bond or changes a side chain. Then verify the product's carbon skeleton.
points: Alcohol → halide · Replace C–O group · Substrate-dependent
Alkene + HX · Consume C=C · Addition pathway
Toluene chlorination · Ring or side chain · Catalyst versus light

chapters.title: SN2: concerted attack and rate
chapters.formula: Rate = k[substrate][nucleophile]
chapters.script: In the S N two mechanism, a nucleophile approaches carbon from the side opposite the leaving group. Bond formation and departure occur in one concerted step. A free carbocation is not an intermediate. In the simple rate law, rate equals the rate constant times substrate concentration times nucleophile concentration. Doubling either concentration doubles the rate, and doubling both multiplies it by four, with temperature and other conditions unchanged. Backside access becomes harder as the reaction centre is crowded. Comparable methyl and primary alkyl substrates are therefore more accessible than tertiary substrates for this pathway. Polar aprotic solvents often support reactive anionic nucleophiles, although the complete substrate and reagent combination must still be considered. At a reacting stereogenic carbon, backside attack inverts the local geometry. This does not automatically turn every R label into S, because priority rankings may change in the product. Reassign the configuration rather than treating a label as a physical mechanism. A stronger nucleophile cannot simply force an ordinary tertiary centre to follow a favourable backside substitution path.
points: Double substrate · 2 · First order in substrate
Double nucleophile · 2 · First order in nucleophile
Double both · 4 · Multiply independent factors

chapters.title: SN1: ionization, capture and rearrangement
chapters.formula: Ideal rate = k[substrate]
chapters.script: In a simple S N one mechanism, slow ionization first forms a carbocation and leaving group. Nucleophile capture occurs afterward. The ideal rate law depends on substrate concentration alone, because nucleophile participation is not part of the slow ionization step. Doubling only nucleophile concentration therefore produces no direct rate change in this ideal model. A tertiary substrate can favour ionization under suitable conditions because its carbocation is more stable than a simple primary one. Benzylic and allylic intermediates may gain resonance stabilization. Strongly ionizing media can assist separation of charged species. A carbocation can rearrange when a more favourable structure is accessible, so compare skeletons before declaring the final substitution product. A planar carbocation permits attack from either face, allowing a stereogenic substrate to lose optical purity. Exact equal racemization is not guaranteed because ion pairing and nearby groups can make the faces unequally accessible. These are mechanistic tendencies, not a rule that every tertiary halide always gives substitution: elimination can compete. State the solvent, nucleophile and temperature before choosing a dominant pathway.
points: Slow ionization · Carbocation formed · Rearrangement possible
Rate = k[R–X] · Substrate-dependent · Nu doubling: factor 1
Planar intermediate · Two faces accessible · Optical purity may fall

chapters.title: Elimination competes with substitution
chapters.formula: E2 removes β-H and leaving group together
chapters.script: In beta elimination, hydrogen is removed from a carbon adjacent to the carbon carrying the leaving group. A double bond forms between these alpha and beta carbons. In the E two mechanism, base removes hydrogen as the leaving group departs in the same step. The simple rate depends on both substrate and base concentrations. An appropriate anti periplanar arrangement helps the required orbital overlap; ring conformations can therefore restrict which product forms. Heating a suitable haloalkane with alcoholic potassium hydroxide commonly favours elimination in elementary questions, while aqueous hydroxide often favours substitution for suitable substrates. These are contextual comparisons, not absolute switches. Bromoethane with aqueous hydroxide can give ethanol; with hot alcoholic base it can give ethene. A secondary butyl halide with a small base often gives but two ene as the major alkene, while bulky bases or geometric restrictions can change preferences. First check that a beta hydrogen exists, then identify all possible adjacent double bonds. Distinguish the major product from the only possible product.
points: Aqueous OH⁻ · Ethanol; substitution · 2 carbons retained
Hot alcoholic base · Ethene; elimination · 2 carbons retained
E2 elementary law · k[R–X][base] · Concerted process

chapters.title: Haloarenes and activated aromatic substitution
chapters.formula: Chlorobenzene is not benzyl chloride
chapters.script: Ordinary chlorobenzene resists the usual alkyl substitution pathways. The chlorine bearing carbon is sp two hybridized, and conjugation gives the carbon chlorine bond partial double bond character. Ordinary backside S N two displacement at that aromatic carbon is difficult. A simple S N one route would require an unfavourable phenyl cation, so it is not the usual alternative. Benzyl chloride has its leaving group on a saturated carbon outside the ring and must be considered separately. Resistance does not mean all haloarenes are chemically inert. Strong electron withdrawing groups, such as nitro groups in suitable ortho or para positions relative to halogen, can activate a ring toward nucleophilic aromatic substitution. The intermediate and reaction pathway differ from ordinary alkyl substitution. A meta nitro group does not provide the same direct resonance stabilization in the usual addition elimination mechanism. Harsh conditions can also allow other aromatic substitution pathways. For an exam comparison, mark the exact attachment point, locate activating substituents and read the conditions before ranking reactivity from a memorized halide list.
points: Aryl C–Cl · Resists alkyl SN1/SN2 · Unfavourable ordinary paths
Benzylic C–Cl · Different reaction centre · Outside ring carbon
Ortho / para nitro · Can activate aromatic SN · Different mechanism

chapters.title: Grignard formation and carbon coupling
chapters.formula: R–MgX + H₂O → R–H + Mg(OH)X
chapters.script: An appropriate organic halide can react with magnesium in dry ether to form a Grignard reagent. Its carbon has strongly basic and nucleophilic character. Water or another sufficiently acidic proton can quench the reagent before a planned carbon carbon bond forming reaction. Ethylmagnesium bromide meeting water gives ethane as its organic product: the ethyl carbon accepts a proton instead of adding to a later carbonyl reagent. This is why dry conditions are chemically necessary. When no acidic interference is present, reaction with an appropriate carbonyl compound followed by work-up can form a new carbon carbon bond, but the precise product depends on the carbonyl partner. Wurtz coupling instead uses sodium with suitable alkyl halides in dry ether. Two methyl halide units can couple to ethane. Using different alkyl halides can give several homo and cross coupling products, making the method poorly selective for one unsymmetrical alkane. Count the carbons from both coupling partners and consider all pairings. Do not confuse magnesium insertion with sodium coupling merely because both start from an organic halide.
points: Ethyl–MgBr + water · Ethane · Proton transfer quenches
2 methyl halide units · Ethane by coupling · Na; dry ether
Mixed Wurtz partners · Several combinations · Poor single-product selectivity

chapters.title: Compound properties and final reaction checks
chapters.formula: Substrate + reagent + solvent + conditions
chapters.script: Some halogen compounds are studied for their properties and environmental history as well as their reactions. Chloroform has been used as a solvent and historically as an anaesthetic. It has significant toxicity and can oxidize in air and light to phosgene. Iodoform is associated with an older antiseptic use and with the yellow product formed in the iodoform test for suitable precursors. Many chlorofluorocarbons persist long enough to reach the stratosphere, where chlorine radicals can catalyse ozone destruction. D D T has a history of insecticidal use and concerns involving persistence and bioaccumulation. These chemical facts should be connected with molecular stability and reaction pathways rather than reduced to a list of names. For a product question, record four things: substrate, reagent, solvent and conditions. Decide whether substitution, elimination, proton transfer or coupling is plausible. Check the carbon skeleton, charges and the presence of beta hydrogen where required. Apply a rate law only to the stated mechanism. The practice questions review those choices; fuller stereochemical drawings and additional preparation routes remain for further lessons.
points: Chloroform · Solvent; historical anaesthetic · Toxicity; air oxidation
CFCs · Ozone destruction · Persistent; radical chemistry
DDT · Insecticide history · Persistence; bioaccumulation

chapters.title: SN2 inversion concerns spatial arrangement
chapters.formula: Backside attack → inversion at the reacting stereogenic carbon
chapters.script: An S N two substitution occurs through a concerted bond making and bond breaking event. The incoming nucleophile approaches opposite the leaving group, producing inversion of the spatial arrangement at a reacting stereogenic carbon. This is often called Walden inversion. It does not imply that every printed R descriptor must change to S, because replacing a group can change the priority order used to assign the descriptor. First follow the actual three dimensional arrangement, then assign priorities to the product. A methyl substrate has no stereogenic carbon, so its S N two reaction cannot be described as producing a pair of carbon enantiomers merely because backside attack occurred. The bimolecular rate law refers to the elementary substitution step and depends on both substrate and nucleophile concentration under that model. Steric crowding near the reacting carbon can hinder the required approach. A tertiary substrate therefore does not become a good ordinary S N two substrate just because a strong nucleophile is present. Separate reaction mechanism, spatial inversion and the final naming descriptor rather than treating them as one memorized word.
points: Concerted substitution · Backside approach · Spatial inversion
R / S naming · Reassign product priorities · Do not switch blindly
Methyl carbon · Not stereogenic · No enantiomer pair here

chapters.title: SN1 stereochemistry and rearrangements
chapters.formula: Planar carbocation permits attack from either face
chapters.script: An S N one model begins with ionization to a carbocation and a leaving group. A simple trigonal planar carbocation can be approached from either face, so substitution at a suitable stereogenic centre can give both configurations. The result is often described as racemization, but real ion pairs and solvent cages can make the proportions unequal. Do not promise an exact fifty fifty mixture without the additional assumptions needed for equal access. Carbocation intermediates can also rearrange by suitable hydride or alkyl shifts when a more favourable cation is accessible. Such a shift moves a bonding pair together with the migrating group and changes which carbon bears the positive charge. It is not a resonance contributor that leaves every hydrogen attachment unchanged. Product prediction therefore needs the substrate structure and conditions, rather than the S N one label alone. The rate determining ionization model gives first order dependence on substrate when that step controls the observed rate. A favourable carbocation does not exclude competing elimination, especially when the surrounding conditions encourage proton removal.
points: Carbocation geometry · Approximately planar · Two faces accessible
Observed products · Ion pairs can matter · Not always exactly 50:50
Rearrangement · Bonded group migrates · Connectivity can change

chapters.title: Substitution and elimination compete
chapters.formula: Aqueous / alcoholic base is a clue, not a universal guarantee
chapters.script: An alkyl halide may undergo substitution or elimination, and the reagent label alone is not a complete prediction. In a common introductory comparison, aqueous hydroxide can replace bromide in bromoethane to give ethanol, while heated alcoholic base can promote elimination to ethene. Both products retain the two carbon skeleton, but they change different bonds. Substitution makes a new carbon oxygen bond; elimination removes a beta hydrogen and the leaving group to form a carbon carbon double bond. A beta hydrogen must be available for this ordinary elimination. With more substituted substrates, base strength and size, solvent, temperature and geometry influence the competition and alkene distribution. In an E two process, the relevant beta carbon hydrogen bond and carbon leaving group bond favour an antiperiplanar arrangement. A bulky base can alter which beta hydrogen is removed, so a single major alkene rule is not universal. Methyl halides lack a beta carbon and cannot undergo the usual beta elimination to an alkene. Inspect the actual substrate and competing paths before using a preparation shortcut.
points: Bromoethane · Aqueous OH⁻ example · Ethanol by substitution
Bromoethane · Heated alcoholic base · Ethene by elimination
Methyl halide · No beta carbon · No ordinary β elimination

chapters.title: Ambidentate cyanide and carbon counting
chapters.formula: R–CN differs from R–NC; nitrile hydrolysis retains its added carbon
chapters.script: An ambidentate reagent can connect through different atoms, so product connectivity matters. In the usual introductory alkyl halide comparison, ionic cyanide such as potassium cyanide favours carbon bonded nitrile formation, while silver cyanide is associated with isocyanide formation through nitrogen under the specified preparation conditions. Do not draw those products as interchangeable resonance forms. For bromoethane reacting by nitrile formation, the two carbon ethyl group acquires the cyanide carbon, producing propanenitrile with three carbons. Subsequent nitrile hydrolysis can give propanoic acid after the appropriate workup. Carbon counting exposes a common error: the product is not ethanoic acid merely because the starting halide was ethyl. An isocyanide has the alkyl group attached to nitrogen instead and requires separate reaction reasoning. These are reagent dependent preparation patterns, not a claim that every substrate reacts equally well. The normal nucleophilic substitution limitations still apply, particularly steric hindrance for a direct S N two pathway. Always identify the atom making the new bond before naming the product or planning the next conversion.
points: Ethyl halide + KCN · C attachment · Propanenitrile; 3 C
Ethyl halide + AgCN · N attachment pattern · Ethyl isocyanide
Propanenitrile hydrolysis · Retain nitrile carbon · Propanoic acid

chapters.title: Aryl, vinyl and benzyl halides differ
chapters.formula: Classify the carbon directly bonded to halogen
chapters.script: A halogen attached directly to an aromatic ring is aryl, while one attached to an alkene carbon is vinylic. A benzyl halide instead has the halogen on a saturated carbon directly next to the aromatic ring. These positions are not equivalent. Benzyl chloride contains a carbon chlorine bond at an S P three carbon, whereas chlorobenzene attaches chlorine to an aromatic S P two carbon. Ordinary alkyl substitution shortcuts cannot simply be transferred to chlorobenzene or a vinyl halide. In an aryl carbon halogen bond, conjugation and the geometry of the carbon framework affect reactivity. Suitable activating substituents and forcing conditions can enable other aromatic substitution pathways, but that does not establish a normal freely formed phenyl carbocation mechanism. Benzyl substrates can be reactive in substitution because their adjacent aromatic system can stabilize relevant intermediates or transition states, subject to the actual pathway and substituents. Classify the reaction centre first, then inspect the nucleophile, solvent and activation pattern. The presence of a benzene ring somewhere in the molecule is not enough to classify every carbon halogen bond as aryl.
points: Chlorobenzene · Cl directly on ring · Aryl C–Cl
Vinyl chloride · Cl on C=C carbon · Vinylic C–Cl
Benzyl chloride · Ph–CH₂–Cl · Benzylic sp³ C–Cl

chapters.title: Halogen exchange depends on the substrate and medium
chapters.formula: Finkelstein: alkyl chloride/bromide → iodide; Swarts: alkyl fluoride
chapters.script: A named reaction is a useful map only when the substrate and conditions match. In the standard Finkelstein comparison, an appropriate alkyl chloride or bromide undergoes halogen exchange with iodide in acetone. The sodium chloride or bromide formed has low solubility in this medium, so its precipitation helps drive the exchange. For a suitable primary substrate, the substitution can follow a concerted backside attack. The carbon skeleton stays unchanged: a two carbon alkyl bromide gives a two carbon alkyl iodide, rather than adding the iodide as a new carbon fragment. The Swarts name instead refers to preparing alkyl fluorides by halogen exchange using suitable metal fluorides. These labels do not make every aryl or vinyl halide behave like a primary alkyl substrate. Chlorobenzene, for example, does not enter ordinary backside substitution at its ring carbon simply because iodide is present. Nor should a solvent precipitation argument be transferred to water without checking salt solubilities. Use the reaction names to identify the exchanged atom, the preserved carbon framework and the stated substrate class. Product bookkeeping is different from an experimental preparation protocol.
points: Finkelstein comparison · R–Br or R–Cl with iodide · R–I; same carbon skeleton
Acetone medium · Low salt solubility · Precipitation assists exchange
Swarts comparison · Suitable metal fluoride · Alkyl fluoride; not R–I

chapters.title: Mixed Wurtz coupling is not automatically selective
chapters.formula: R–X and R′–X can give R–R, R–R′ and R′–R′
chapters.script: Carbon coupling needs a selectivity check as well as a carbon count. In the elementary Wurtz scheme, two alkyl halide fragments couple in the presence of sodium, with salt as another product. If only one suitable alkyl halide is used, joining two identical fragments gives a symmetrical alkane. Mixing methyl and ethyl halides does not guarantee pure propane. The possible simple coupling connectivities are methyl with methyl, methyl with ethyl, and ethyl with ethyl, giving ethane, propane and butane respectively. The two possible orders of joining methyl to ethyl describe the same propane connectivity, not two different constitutional products. Thus the elementary list contains three alkane connectivities, not four. This count is not a prediction of equal amounts or a fixed statistical yield. Different substrate reactivities, side reactions and conditions affect the actual product mixture. Wurtz coupling is generally more useful for an appropriate symmetrical target than as an unqualified route to one unsymmetrical alkane from a mixed feed. Balance two sodium atoms for two halide ions in the simple overall coupling equation, and keep product identity separate from an assumed product distribution.
points: Methyl + methyl · 1 + 1 carbon atoms · Ethane: C₂
Methyl + ethyl · 1 + 2 carbon atoms · Propane: C₃
Ethyl + ethyl · 2 + 2 carbon atoms · Butane: C₄; amounts not fixed

chapters.title: Grignard addition combines two carbon ledgers
chapters.formula: CH₃MgBr + CH₃CHO, then protonation → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃
chapters.script: An organomagnesium reagent contributes its carbon fragment to a carbonyl compound in the familiar Grignard addition model. Take methylmagnesium bromide and acetaldehyde, followed by a separate protonation step. The carbon bearing magnesium forms a bond to the former carbonyl carbon. Acetaldehyde supplies two carbon atoms and the methyl fragment supplies one, giving a three carbon alcohol, propan two ol. The carbonyl oxygen becomes an alkoxide oxygen first and is protonated later; the alcohol proton need not come from the original aldehyde. Compare a methyl reagent with formaldehyde: one plus one carbon gives ethanol, a primary alcohol. With propanone, three plus one gives a four carbon tertiary alcohol. These examples classify the alcohol by the groups on its oxygen bearing carbon, not by the total carbon count alone. Water or another suitable proton donor present before addition can instead consume the organomagnesium reagent through an acid base reaction, producing the corresponding hydrocarbon. Therefore carbonyl addition and proton quenching are competing descriptions only after the order of exposure is specified. This is a connectivity and stoichiometry exercise, not a laboratory handling recipe.
points: Methyl fragment + formaldehyde · 1 + 1 carbons · Ethanol; primary
Methyl fragment + acetaldehyde · 1 + 2 carbons · Propan-2-ol; secondary
Methyl fragment + propanone · 1 + 3 carbons · 2-Methylpropan-2-ol; tertiary

chapters.title: Count substitution and elimination products separately
chapters.formula: 2-Bromobutane: substitution gives butan-2-ol; elimination can give butenes
chapters.script: A product count must state whether it counts connectivity or stereochemistry. Consider two bromobutane as a substrate and compare idealized substitution with elimination. Replacing bromine by hydroxyl at the same carbon gives butan two ol as the substitution connectivity. In elimination, removing a beta hydrogen from either adjacent carbon can place the double bond at the end of the chain or in its middle. The constitutional alkene products are but one ene and but two ene. The internal alkene has two distinct groups at each double bond carbon, so it can occur as E and Z geometrical isomers. The terminal alkene has a carbon bearing two hydrogens and therefore has no E Z pair. Counting alkene stereoisomers separately gives three alkene products in this elementary set, while counting alkene connectivities gives two. This enumeration does not claim that all are formed in equal amounts or that substitution is absent under every elimination condition. Base size, solvent, temperature and the available conformations affect competition and selectivity. In an E two pathway, the removed hydrogen and leaving group require a suitable antiperiplanar arrangement; a flat formula alone does not determine the relative yields.
points: Substitution connectivity · Replace Br by OH · Butan-2-ol
Elimination connectivities · Double bond at C1 or C2 · But-1-ene; but-2-ene
Resolve alkene geometry · But-2-ene has E and Z · 3 alkene stereoisomers total

chapters.title: Alcohol activation changes the leaving group problem
chapters.formula: 3ROH + PBr₃ → 3RBr + H₃PO₃ in the net conversion model
chapters.script: An alcohol does not usually undergo a simple substitution by expelling free hydroxide without activation. For suitable primary and secondary alcohols, phosphorus tribromide can enable conversion of the carbon oxygen bond into a carbon bromine bond. The net bookkeeping equation uses three alcohol molecules for one phosphorus tribromide, forming three alkyl bromides and phosphorous acid. This balances oxygen and hydrogen as well as bromine. For a stipulated quantitative conversion of zero point zero three zero zero mole ethanol, the theoretical phosphorus tribromide amount from this equation is zero point zero one zero zero mole and bromoethane amount zero point zero three zero zero mole. This is stoichiometric bookkeeping, not a complete experimental reagent prescription. A suitable secondary stereogenic alcohol can undergo inversion at the reacting carbon in the usual substitution pathway. That does not imply an automatic reversal of its R or S letter without checking product priorities. Tertiary substrates do not follow this same simple backside displacement model. Choose the actual substrate class and leaving group activation before copying a reagent rule onto every alcohol.

chapters.title: Two eliminations from a dihalide make a triple bond
chapters.formula: BrCH₂CH₂Br − 2HBr → HC≡CH as formal atom accounting
chapters.script: A vicinal dihalide contains halogens on adjacent carbon atoms. In an appropriate double dehydrohalogenation sequence, two eliminations can convert that skeleton into an alkyne. For one two dibromoethane, the starting formula is two carbons, four hydrogens and two bromines. Removing two hydrogen bromide units leaves two carbons and two hydrogens, the formula of ethyne. The first elimination produces a vinyl halide with a carbon carbon double bond. The second elimination acts on that different bonding environment and generally requires a suitably strong base; it is not simply a repeat of the easiest alkyl halide reaction. The overall carbon count remains two. Formal loss of two hydrogen bromide units counts the two elimination events, but does not establish that exactly two equivalents of base suffice in every preparative system. A terminal alkyne can also undergo deprotonation by a sufficiently strong base, followed by separate protonation on workup. Distinguish transformation stoichiometry, intermediate identity and reagent consumption rather than treating a net atom ledger as a complete mechanism or procedure.

chapters.title: Carbon dioxide and proton quenching give different Grignard products
chapters.formula: RMgX + CO₂, then protonation → RCOOH; proton quench → RH
chapters.script: The fate of a Grignard reagent depends on whether it meets a carbon electrophile or a proton source. Ethylmagnesium bromide contains a two carbon organic group. Addition to carbon dioxide followed by separate protonation gives propanoic acid, whose carboxyl carbon came from carbon dioxide. The product has three carbons. Direct proton quenching of the same reagent instead gives ethane, retaining only the original two carbons. Phenylmagnesium bromide similarly gives benzoic acid after carbon dioxide addition and protonation, so six ring carbons become a seven carbon acid. These transformations do not imply that a carboxylic acid itself is an interchangeable carbon dioxide reagent: an acidic proton can consume the organomagnesium reagent by acid base reaction. The initial addition product in carboxylation is a metal carboxylate, not the fully protonated acid. Other acidic groups or reactive functions in the substrate can prevent a simple Grignard route. Track the source of the added carbon and the timing of protonation before choosing between a carbon forming reaction and a reagent destroying quench.
points: Ethylmagnesium bromide: two C · CO₂ addition, then protonation · Propanoic acid: three C
Same ethyl reagent · Direct proton source · Ethane: two C
Phenylmagnesium bromide: six C · CO₂ supplies carboxyl carbon · Benzoic acid: seven C

chapters.title: Halogens deactivate a ring but direct ortho and para
chapters.formula: Electrophilic substitution: halogen is deactivating and ortho/para directing
chapters.script: A substituent can influence overall reaction speed and positional preference in different ways. In ordinary electrophilic aromatic substitution, chlorine withdraws electron density inductively, making chlorobenzene less reactive than benzene under comparable conditions. Yet its lone pairs can contribute resonance stabilization to the intermediates for ortho and para attack relative to meta attack. Thus a halogen is a deactivating ortho and para director, not an activating group merely because of those preferred positions. For a simple nitration comparison, ortho and para chloronitrobenzene are the usual favoured positional products, while the carbon chlorine bond remains intact. This is not nucleophilic aromatic substitution, where a nucleophile replaces the leaving group under an appropriate activation pattern. Nor does an ortho para label specify a universal numerical product ratio. Steric effects, electrophile identity and reaction conditions affect the distribution. Keep three separate questions visible: what kind of substitution occurs, which bond changes, and how the existing substituent affects rate and position. A single directing arrow cannot answer all three.
points: Chlorobenzene in electrophilic substitution · Net inductive withdrawal · Less reactive than benzene
Relative positional preference · Lone-pair resonance contributions · Ortho / para directing
Ring nitration versus aryl substitution · Ring H replaced versus C–Cl replaced · Different reaction classes

quiz.question: Which has chlorine directly attached to an aromatic-ring carbon?
quiz.explanation: Chlorobenzene has an aryl C-Cl bond; benzyl chloride has chlorine on an external saturated carbon.

quiz.question: A simple SN2 mechanism contains:
quiz.explanation: Backside bond formation and leaving-group departure occur together rather than through a free carbocation.

quiz.question: In the ideal SN1 rate law, doubling only nucleophile concentration changes rate by:
quiz.explanation: The ideal law depends on substrate concentration because its slow ionization precedes nucleophile capture.

quiz.question: SN2 at a reacting stereogenic carbon gives:
quiz.explanation: Backside attack inverts the local arrangement; R/S labels must be reassigned using the product priorities.

quiz.question: Water added to a Grignard reagent generally:
quiz.explanation: The strongly basic carbon accepts a proton, producing a hydrocarbon and destroying the organomagnesium reagent.

quiz.question: The hydrogen removed in a beta elimination is on:
options: A carbon adjacent to the carbon carrying X
quiz.explanation: Removing beta hydrogen and the alpha leaving group forms a double bond between adjacent carbons.

quiz.question: For rate = k[R-X][Nu], doubling both concentrations changes rate by:
quiz.explanation: The two independent factors of two multiply to four.

quiz.question: Under standard elementary conditions, bromoethane with hot alcoholic KOH mainly undergoes:
options: Formation of ethyne in one step
quiz.explanation: Base removes beta hydrogen while bromide leaves, forming the two-carbon alkene.

quiz.question: Which nitro position can provide the usual resonance activation for nucleophilic aromatic displacement of ring halogen?
quiz.explanation: Ortho and para nitro groups can stabilize the intermediate in the usual addition-elimination pathway.

quiz.question: Why is mixed-halide Wurtz coupling often poorly selective for one unsymmetrical alkane?
options: Several homo- and cross-coupling pairings can occur
Every substrate must become an alcohol
quiz.explanation: Different starting halides permit multiple coupling combinations.

quiz.question: An SN2 reaction at a stereogenic carbon directly implies:
options: Guaranteed R → S in every naming case
quiz.explanation: Backside displacement gives inversion; changed CIP priorities can affect the final R/S label.

quiz.question: A real SN1 reaction gives both configurations at a reacting centre. Their proportions:
options: Can differ because ion pairs and solvent cages matter
quiz.explanation: Planar access supports both configurations, but real environments need not give equal face access.

quiz.question: Which substrate lacks a beta carbon for ordinary beta elimination?
quiz.explanation: The methyl substrate has no neighbouring carbon carrying a beta hydrogen.

quiz.question: Bromoethane → nitrile using ionic cyanide → acid by hydrolysis gives:
quiz.explanation: The cyanide carbon adds one to the two-carbon ethyl skeleton and remains in the acid.

quiz.question: In benzyl chloride Ph–CH2–Cl, chlorine is bonded to:
quiz.explanation: The reacting C–Cl carbon is sp3 and adjacent to the aromatic ring.

quiz.question: The connectivity R–CN versus R–NC distinguishes:
quiz.explanation: The alkyl group is bonded to carbon in the nitrile and to nitrogen in the isocyanide.

quiz.question: A suitable alkyl bromide undergoes Finkelstein exchange with iodide. The carbon skeleton:
quiz.explanation: Halogen exchange replaces the halogen; iodide introduces no carbon atom.

quiz.question: In the standard acetone Finkelstein comparison, which effect assists the exchange?
options: Water always supplies an alkyl group
Precipitation of sodium chloride or bromide
quiz.explanation: Low solubility of the product sodium halide in acetone helps remove it from the solution equilibrium.

quiz.question: The elementary alkane connectivity list from mixed methyl and ethyl Wurtz fragments contains:
quiz.explanation: Methyl–methyl, methyl–ethyl and ethyl–ethyl give ethane, propane and butane.

quiz.question: Which statement about that mixed coupling product list follows from connectivity alone?
options: Propane must be the only product
quiz.explanation: Enumeration identifies possible connectivities but supplies no kinetics or selectivity data.

quiz.question: Methylmagnesium bromide adds to acetaldehyde before protonation. The alcohol is:
quiz.explanation: The methyl fragment contributes one carbon to the two-carbon aldehyde, giving a secondary three-carbon alcohol.

quiz.question: Methyl addition to propanone followed by protonation gives an alcohol whose oxygen-bearing carbon is:
quiz.explanation: The oxygen-bearing carbon is bonded to three methyl carbon groups after addition.

quiz.question: The alkene constitutional products of simple elimination from 2-bromobutane are:
quiz.explanation: The two adjacent beta positions place the double bond at C1 or C2 without changing the four-carbon chain.

quiz.question: Counting E/Z separately, that elementary butene set contains:
quiz.explanation: But-1-ene contributes one and but-2-ene contributes E and Z; this is a count, not a yield claim.

quiz.question: In the net model 3ROH+PBr3→3RBr+H3PO3, converting 0.0300 mol suitable alcohol theoretically uses PBr3 amount:
quiz.explanation: The balanced net equation has three alcohol molecules per PBr3, so 0.0300/3=0.0100 mol.

quiz.question: The simple PBr3 backside-substitution model is most appropriate for:
quiz.explanation: Substrate class matters; the usual primary/secondary substitution pathway cannot simply be imposed on tertiary centres.

quiz.question: Formal loss of 2HBr from C2H4Br2 leaves formula:
quiz.explanation: Subtract two hydrogens and two bromines from the vicinal dihalide formula; the two carbon atoms remain.

quiz.question: The intermediate after one elimination from 1,2-dibromoethane is a:
quiz.explanation: One elimination creates a double bond while leaving one halogen; the second elimination acts on a vinyl-halide environment.

quiz.question: Ethylmagnesium bromide reacts with CO2 and is then protonated. The organic acid has:
quiz.explanation: The two-carbon ethyl group gains the carboxyl carbon supplied by carbon dioxide, giving propanoic acid.

quiz.question: Direct proton quenching of ethylmagnesium bromide instead gives:
quiz.explanation: A proton source converts the ethyl group to ethane without adding a carbon atom.

quiz.question: In ordinary electrophilic aromatic substitution, chlorine on benzene is:
quiz.explanation: Net inductive withdrawal reduces overall reactivity, while resonance effects favour ortho/para over meta attack.

quiz.question: In nitration of chlorobenzene, the usual substitution changes:
options: Every ring bond into a single bond
A ring C–H bond while C–Cl remains
quiz.explanation: Electrophilic ring substitution replaces a ring hydrogen; it is distinct from nucleophilic replacement of the aryl halogen.
